displayQuote: Behind every great fortune there is a crime

meta.title: Who really said "Behind every great fortune there is a crime"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Balzac's wording. In Le Père Goriot his character Vautrin says something narrower; the maxim was in print by 1912 and Puzo's Godfather fixed it in 1969.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Behind every great fortune there is a crime'?
meta.ogDescription: Balzac wrote a narrower line in Le Père Goriot. The famous compressed version is an anonymous paraphrase, in print by 1912, popularized by The Godfather.

answer.label: Not Balzac’s wording — a simplified paraphrase
answer.authorDates: 1799–1850 · French novelist · wrote a narrower version of this line
answer.sourceLine: Balzac did write about fortunes and crime, but not this sentence: in Le Père Goriot (serialized 1834–35) the escaped convict Vautrin tells a broke law student that a great fortune with no visible cause conceals a crime committed neatly — a claim about a subset, not about every fortune. Quote Investigator ↗ could not locate the compressed maxim in any work Balzac wrote and concludes it evolved through decades of retelling, with no single author.

source.heading: What Balzac actually wrote

Ellen Marriage, 1896 (J. M. Dent, London), p. 124

source.excerpt:
Despise mankind and find out the meshes that you can slip through in the net of the Code. The secret of a great success for which you are at a loss to account is a crime that has never been found out, because it was properly executed.”

“Silence, sir! I will not hear any more; you make me doubt myself.
trail: 1834–35 — Balzac gives Vautrin the sentence in Le Père Goriot, immediately after a rant about how the Code punishes the crude thief and spares the polished one. Read it in the French original ↗.

1896 and 1900 — the two standard English translations, by Ellen Marriage and by Katharine Prescott Wormeley, both keep the qualifier about fortunes with no apparent cause; neither produces the popular slogan. Both are transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗, and Marriage’s is free at Project Gutenberg ↗.

1912 to 1958 — the maxim circulates in shrinking forms: an unnamed “French writer” in 1912, a hedged “I think it was Balzac” from Sir James Henry Yoxall in 1925, then C. Wright Mills’s The Power Elite in 1956 attaching it firmly to Balzac — all dated and sourced by QI ↗.
1969 — Mario Puzo prints the wording we use today as the epigraph to The Godfather, signed simply “—Balzac,” per Wikipedia ↗. After that the paraphrase is unstoppable.
source.excerptNote: The French original reads: Le secret des grandes fortunes sans cause apparente est un crime oublié, parce qu’il a été proprement fait. Note the qualifier — sans cause apparente, without apparent cause. No translation of Balzac renders this as “Behind every great fortune there is a crime.”

sourceLink.text: Father Goriot, translated by Ellen Marriage — full text at Project Gutenberg

source.rightsNote: The two texts shown here are safely out of copyright: Balzac’s French original was published in 1834–35, and Ellen Marriage’s English translation dates from 1896 — Project Gutenberg ↗ hosts it as public domain in the USA. The famous one-liner is a different matter: it is not from either text, has no identifiable author or first publication to attach rights to, and its best-known appearance — the epigraph to The Godfather (1969) — sits in a book that remains in copyright. We therefore assert no rights status for the popular wording.

author.name: Honoré de Balzac
author.heading: Honoré de Balzac
author.metaLine: 1799–1850 · French novelist · author of La Comédie humaine
author.bio: Balzac (born in Tours on 20 May 1799, died in Paris on 18 August 1850) built La Comédie humaine, a linked sequence of novels and stories that Wikipedia ↗ describes as a panorama of post-Napoleonic French life. He is regarded as one of the founders of European literary realism, and his trick of letting the same characters reappear across books — Vautrin and Rastignac among them — is part of why his lines circulate detached from their speakers. The sentence people quote as his was never his; the sharper, narrower one he actually wrote is put in the mouth of a criminal who is trying to corrupt someone.

cite.sourceCitation: Honoré de Balzac, “Le Père Goriot,” Revue de Paris 12 (1834): 258; English as Father Goriot, trans. Ellen Marriage (London: J. M. Dent, 1896), 124. The popular wording “Behind every great fortune there is a crime” appears in no work by Balzac; see Quote Investigator, “Quote Origin: Behind Every Great Fortune There Is a Crime,” 9 September 2013.

copyAttribution: "Behind every great fortune there is a crime" is not Balzac's wording and appears in none of his works. In Le Pere Goriot (serialized 1834-35) the criminal Vautrin says, in Ellen Marriage's 1896 translation: "The secret of a great success for which you are at a loss to account is a crime that has never been found out, because it was properly executed." A compressed form was already in print by 1912, credited only to an unnamed French writer, and Mario Puzo's 1969 epigraph to The Godfather fixed the modern wording under Balzac's name. — Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Who really said it
misattribution.intro: Almost every printing of this line carries Balzac’s name, and the name is not baseless — but the sentence is not a translation of anything he wrote. It is the end point of a long compression, and the people who did the compressing are mostly anonymous.

items.why: Balzac’s sentence is narrower and conditional — it concerns great fortunes sans cause apparente, those with no visible source. Quote Investigator ↗ states plainly that Balzac did not pronounce a general rule, and that it could not find the compressed maxim in any work he wrote.

A Paris dispatch by Pierre Mille, printed in the Charleston News and Courier on 18 May 1912, has a dinner guest at London’s Carlton Hotel quoting “At the base of every great fortune there is a great crime” and crediting only an unnamed French writer — documented by QI ↗. Balzac’s name is absent.

items.who: C. Wright Mills, then Mario Puzo
items.why: Mills’s The Power Elite (1956) credited Balzac with “behind every great fortune there lies a crime,” and Puzo used the exact modern wording as the epigraph of The Godfather — Wikipedia ↗ notes he “opened his 1969 novel with an epigraph popularly attributed to Balzac.”

Wikiquote ↗ suggests the “great crime” variant may have originated in The Oil Barons: Men of Greed and Grandeur (1971) by Richard O’Connor, p. 47. That cannot be where it began: QI ↗ prints the same compressed phrasing from 1912, and Wikiquote itself notes the line was already in The Godfather two years earlier.

misattribution.truthLine: Balzac wrote something narrower, sharper and better — and gave it to a criminal to say. The absolute version everyone quotes is an anonymous compression that Quote Investigator ↗ credits to no single person.

context.heading: What Vautrin was actually arguing
lead: The line lands very differently once you know who says it. In Le Père Goriot the speaker is Vautrin — a master criminal living under a false name in a shabby Paris boarding house — and he is mid-seduction, trying to talk the impoverished student Rastignac into a scheme that ends in a duel and a dead man. His point is not a law of economics. It is: the law punishes the poor thief and lets the polished one alone, so look for the gaps in the net. The French text ↗ puts the sentence at the end of that pitch, and Rastignac’s reply is to beg him to stop talking.

Balzac’s version is also carefully hedged: it is about fortunes sans cause apparente — the ones with no visible source. The compressed maxim drops that qualifier and turns a novelist’s observation into a universal indictment. Wikipedia ↗ calls the popular form a somewhat inaccurate paraphrase, which is about right: it is more quotable and less true.
context.detailsSummary: How the sentence got shorter, decade by decade
detailsBody: 1834–35 — Balzac publishes the original in Le Père Goriot: a forgotten crime behind fortunes without apparent cause.

1912 — a newspaper account by Pierre Mille of a London dinner quotes a guest citing an unnamed “French writer”: “At the base of every great fortune there is a great crime.” Balzac is not named. Documented by Quote Investigator ↗.
1925 — Sir James Henry Yoxall writes “Somebody said—I think it was Balzac—that at the root of every great fortune there was a crime,” a hedge that shows the attribution was still loose.
1956 — C. Wright Mills’s The Power Elite credits Balzac with “behind every great fortune there lies a crime,” giving the maxim academic weight.

1969 — Mario Puzo prints “Behind every great fortune there is a crime. —Balzac” as the epigraph of The Godfather. That is the earliest instance of this exact wording in QI’s chronology, and the form everyone now repeats.
context.pull: …a crime that has never been found out, because it was properly executed.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes the adage was inspired by Balzac's sentence in Le Père Goriot (Revue de Paris, 1834) but was simplified over time, states it could not locate the maxim in any Balzac work, and gives a dated chronology: 1912 'At the base of every great fortune there is a great crime' credited to an unidentified 'French writer' (Charleston News and Courier, 18 May 1912, Pierre Mille, Carlton Hotel dinner); 1925 Yoxall 'Somebody said—I think it was Balzac'; 1956 C. Wright Mills, The Power Elite, 'behind every great fortune there lies a crime'; 1958 Daniel Bell; 1969 Puzo's Godfather epigraph 'Behind every great fortune there is a crime.—Balzac'; and that no single person can be credited with the modern version. Also transcribes the 1896 Ellen Marriage and 1900 Katharine Prescott Wormeley translations.

Wikiquote lists 'Le secret des grandes fortunes sans cause apparente est un crime oublié, parce qu'il a été proprement fait' with an English translation under the sourced section heading 'Father Goriot (1835)', and adds a note that the variant 'Behind every great fortune there is a great crime' may have originated in a paraphrase in The Oil Barons: Men of Greed and Grandeur (1971) by Richard O'Connor, p. 47, also noting it appears at the beginning of The Godfather, published two years earlier.

Project Gutenberg's Father Goriot, translator Ellen Marriage, contains Vautrin's speech ending 'Despise mankind and find out the meshes that you can slip through in the net of the Code. The secret of a great success for which you are at a loss to account is a crime that has never been found out, because it was properly executed.' followed by Rastignac's reply 'Silence, sir! I will not hear any more; you make me doubt myself.' The record lists the work as public domain in the USA.

The French original sentence 'Le secret des grandes fortunes sans cause apparente est un crime oublié, parce qu'il a été proprement fait' appears at the close of Vautrin's speech to Rastignac on page 145 of the 1910 edition of Le Père Goriot, immediately after the passage contrasting the dandy's two months in prison with the poor devil's penal servitude; the following exchange identifies the speaker ('dit Vautrin').

Père Goriot was serialized in the Revue de Paris from December 1834 to February 1835 and published as a book in March 1835; Vautrin is a master criminal; and the article notes the line has been 'frequently – and somewhat inaccurately – paraphrased as: Behind every great fortune is a great crime.'

Wikipedia states 'Puzo opened his 1969 novel with an epigraph popularly attributed to Balzac: Behind every great fortune there is a crime,' and that the saying most likely evolved over time from Balzac's original text; publisher G. P. Putnam's Sons, published 10 March 1969.

Honoré de Balzac was born 20 May 1799 in Tours and died 18 August 1850 in Paris; he was a French novelist known for La Comédie humaine, 'a panorama of post-Napoleonic French life', and is regarded as one of the founders of realism in European literature, using recurring characters across works.
